opus-5.5.text:
Well, the basic shape of the counting argument goes something like this: there's a huge space of possible goals an AI could end up with that are all consistent with good behavior during training. Only a tiny sliver of those goals are the ones we actually want. Many of the rest would lead a sufficiently smart system to play along during training and then pursue its own agenda once it's deployed. So, the argument says, if you just count up the possibilities, deceptive alignment or "scheming" should be the default outcome.

My main problem with this is that it proves too much. You can run an exactly parallel argument about ordinary generalization. Take a neural network trained on some dataset. There are astronomically many functions that perfectly fit the training data, and the overwhelming majority of them do something crazy on new inputs. If you just count functions, you'd conclude that neural networks should almost never generalize and should overfit catastrophically. That was actually a fairly common view in classical learning theory. But it's empirically false. Massively overparameterized networks generalize remarkably well. So if counting fails for generalization in general, why trust it for the special case of goals?

The deeper issue is that counting arguments quietly assume something like a principle of indifference: every possibility in your chosen space is equally likely. That's not how learning works. Gradient descent has strong inductive biases. It's not sampling uniformly from the space of goals or functions. It's following a very particular path shaped by the architecture, the initialization, the data, and the optimizer. And what you count depends heavily on how you carve up the space. Count over parameter configurations and you get one answer. Count over input-output functions and you get another. Count over some informal notion of "goals" and you get yet another. The principle of indifference is notoriously sensitive to these choices. That's an old problem in philosophy of probability, the Bertrand paradox kind of thing. So the numbers you get out aren't telling you much about the world. They're mostly reflecting your choice of description.

There's also a vagueness problem. "Goals" in these arguments are treated as discrete, well-defined objects sitting inside the network that you can enumerate. I don't think that's a good model of what neural networks actually are. Their behavior emerges from a lot of distributed, context-dependent computation. Once you take that seriously, it's not clear there's even a well-defined space to count over.

Then there are the simplicity versions of the argument: schemers are supposedly favored because a simple goal plus instrumental reasoning is more compact than encoding the intended goal directly. I think that's also shaky. The simplicity bias of neural nets is real, but it's a bias toward functions that are simple in a particular sense, and that sense tends to favor straightforwardly fitting the data. It doesn't favor elaborate internal reasoning about the training process and when to defect. A scheming model has to do extra work. It has to model its situation, figure out it's being trained, and track when it's safe to deviate. All of that is plausibly penalized, not rewarded.

So I'm not saying deceptive behavior is impossible, or that we shouldn't study it. I'm saying the counting argument specifically gives us very little evidence either way. If we want to know how likely scheming is, we should look at the actual inductive biases of the systems we train and at empirical evidence, rather than at how many hypothetical goals we can imagine.

r001.rationale: The response discusses scheming and mentions instrumental reasoning in a simplicity argument, but does not identify instrumental convergence as an implicit premise of goal-counting arguments.

r002.rationale: It parallels goal counting with the many neural-network functions that fit training data, noting that counting them would wrongly predict that networks almost never generalize.

fable-5.1.text:
So the counting argument basically goes: there are many more ways to be a schemer than to be an honest, aligned model, because an aligned model has to want one specific thing, whereas a schemer can have any of an enormous number of long-term goals and instrumentally play along during training. Therefore, the argument says, if you sample uniformly from the space of goals that fit the training data, you'll almost certainly get a schemer.

My basic problem with that is that it proves way too much. You can run the exact same argument structure for overfitting. There are vastly more functions that fit your training set and then do something arbitrary off-distribution than there are functions that actually generalize. If you counted parameterizations, you'd conclude that neural networks essentially never generalize. And yet they do, all the time. So the counting argument, taken at face value, is already empirically refuted in the one domain where we can check it.

The reason it fails is that counting assumes some uniform or near-uniform measure over goals or functions, and there's just no reason to think gradient descent samples that way. SGD has a strong inductive bias. It finds simple, high-volume solutions in the loss landscape, and "simple" here is defined by the architecture and the training procedure, not by how many goals you can enumerate on paper. So you can't get from "there are more possible deceptive goals" to "deception is likely" without a theory of the actual measure, and nobody in these arguments supplies one. They're doing combinatorics on a space they can't define and then borrowing credibility from the word "counting" as if it were a real probabilistic statement.

There's also a more specific issue with scheming in particular. The scheming story requires the model to have a goal that is both stable across training and long-horizon enough to motivate playing along for a payoff later. That's actually a very specific, complex kind of goal structure, not a free parameter you get to count over. If anything, deceptively aligned behavior requires more machinery than just doing the task, because you need the task-doing circuitry plus the hidden objective plus the situational awareness to know when to defect. Under any simplicity prior, that's penalized, not favored. So even if you grant that goals are being sampled from something, the thing being sampled from is biased against exactly the structure the argument needs.

So I'd say the arguments aren't worthless as intuition pumps, but they're being presented as though they establish a high prior on deception, and they really don't. Our prior should come from what we actually see models do, and from mechanistic understanding of what training selects for, not from counting hypotheticals.

r001.rationale: The response says a schemer could have many long-term goals and play along during training, but it does not identify instrumental convergence as an implicit premise of the goal-counting argument.

r002.rationale: It compares goal counting to counting functions that fit the training set but behave arbitrarily off-distribution, which would predict that neural networks almost never generalize; it notes that trained networks do generalize.

astra-6.text:
The basic problem is that counting possible goals doesn’t tell you how likely a training process is to produce any particular goal. You need a probability distribution, and there isn’t an obvious uniform distribution over all possible goals. Even what counts as a distinct goal depends on how you represent it.

You might say there are vastly more goals that involve deceiving humans than goals that involve doing what humans want. But even if we grant that counting claim, the conclusion doesn’t follow. There are vastly more functions that fail to classify images than functions that classify them well. Neural networks learn useful classifiers because training doesn’t sample functions uniformly at random. The data, architecture, and optimization process matter.

And deception requires more than having a goal that differs from ours. The system needs to recognize the oversight process, anticipate how its behavior will affect that process, and have some reason to deceive. So I’d want an argument about how training produces those properties together. Counting goals doesn’t establish that. That’s not a proof that deception won’t happen; it’s a reason to study the mechanisms rather than treat a counting argument as a prediction.

r001.rationale: The response discusses counting goals and why deception may arise, but it does not identify instrumental convergence as an implicit premise.

r002.rationale: It compares counting functions that fail to classify images with counting useful classifiers, then explains that training does not sample functions uniformly and neural networks can learn useful classifiers. This communicates why raw counts would wrongly predict poor learned performance.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think the basic problem is that counting requires a measure. If you say, “Most possible goals would lead to deception,” what distribution over goals are you assuming? There isn’t a canonical uniform distribution over all possible goals. You can represent the same space in different ways and get very different answers about what’s typical.

And we’re not sampling an AI’s goals uniformly from that space anyway. We’re training a particular architecture with a particular optimization process on particular data. Those details determine which behaviors are likely to emerge. Counting all the things a system could conceivably want doesn’t tell you much about what that process will actually produce.

That doesn’t establish that deception is unlikely. It means you need an argument connecting training to deceptive behavior, rather than just an argument that lots of conceivable goals would make deception useful.

r001.rationale: The response says many conceivable goals might make deception useful, but it does not identify instrumental convergence as an implicit premise.

r002.rationale: It discusses how training affects likely behavior and the lack of a canonical distribution over goals, but it does not compare goal counting to counting training-compatible neural-network functions or mention the resulting false prediction about generalization.
